payload.text: NASA SP-2015-013: A Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science Microgravity Droplet, Gaseous, and Solid Combustion Phenomena in Orbit Experiment: NASA PSI Combustion Science Suite (FLEX, ACME, CIR) Environment: ISS Microgravity Environment (14.7 psi, 21% O2, microgravity) Pressure: 14.7 psi Oxygen %: 21% 1. Microgravity Combustion Fundamentals Combustion accounts for roughly 85 percent of the world's primary energy consumption. On Earth, gravity causes buoyant updrafts that distort flames, complicate numerical simulations, and mask subtle chemical-kinetic and radiative mechanisms. Aboard the International Space Station, experiments within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and Glovebox allow scientists to study spherical droplet burning, low-temperature cool flame chemistry, and solid material ignition without buoyant interference. 2. The FLEX & ACME Discoveries The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) discovered that large hydrocarbon fuel droplets (heptane, decane) burn in two distinct stages in microgravity. After the initial high-temperature (~1800 K) visible flame goes out due to radiative cooling, combustion continues undetected as a quasi-steady 'cool flame' at temperatures between 600 K and 800 K. This low-temperature regime is maintained by low-temperature peroxide chain branching, fundamentally altering our understanding of fuel kinetics and fire detection in space habitats. 3. Physical Science Informatics (PSI) Database Ingestion The NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository archives raw video, spectral radiometry, thermocouple telemetry, and analyzed velocity fields from orbital investigations. Researchers access these open-science datasets to calibrate spacecraft flammability limits and develop clean terrestrial combustion technologies.

payload.title: Elevated-Oxygen Reduced-Pressure Flammability Envelope for Moon Base & Orion
payload.excerpt: Under 10.2 psi and 30% O2 exploration atmospheres, reduced total pressure lowers convective heat loss while elevated O2 raises PMMA and textile spread by ~1.42x.
payload.text: Saffire-IV and exploration-atmosphere screening evaluate Moon Base and Artemis cabin conditions at 10.2 psi total pressure and 30% O2 (70% N2). Lowering total pressure cuts EVA pre-breathe overhead, but reducing nitrogen diluent shrinks heat capacity and increases radiative-convective heat feedback to solid fuels. PMMA and Nomex specimens exhibit lower minimum ignition energy (~0.48 mJ) and ~1.42x higher flame spread rate than sea-level 14.7 psi / 21% O2 air, requiring tighter material screening.

payload.title: Solid Fuel Rod & Sheet Extinction Limits Under Low-Velocity Microgravity Flow
payload.environmentLabel: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (14.7 psi, 21% O2)
payload.excerpt: BASS-II opposed-flow PMMA rods peaked in flame spread at 15-30 cm/s airflow before transitioning to soot-free blue diffusion flamelets near quiescent extinction.
payload.text: Conducted inside the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, BASS-II tested 1-2 cm solid PMMA rods, spheres, and cotton-fiberglass blends under controlled 0-55 cm/s forced flows at 14.7 psi and 16-24% O2. Unlike Saffire's large radiative panels, small BASS-II samples showed a sharp non-monotonic velocity curve: below 10 cm/s, flames turned soot-free blue and relied purely on Fickian molecular oxygen diffusion; at 15-30 cm/s, opposed flow accelerated flame spread before blow-off or radiative quenching occurred.

payload.experiment: BASS-II / PSI-117 (Burning and Suppression of Solids)
payload.title: Nasa Psi 117 Bass2 Combustion Extinction - Section 1
payload.excerpt: NASA PSI-117: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Microgravity Solid Fuel Flammability & Extinction Limits Under Quiescent and Forced Low-Flow Conditions Experiment: BASS-II / PSI-117 Environment: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (14.7 psi, 21% O2, 0.00 g) Pressure...
payload.text: NASA PSI-117: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Microgravity Solid Fuel Flammability & Extinction Limits Under Quiescent and Forced Low-Flow Conditions Experiment: BASS-II / PSI-117 Environment: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (14.7 psi, 21% O2, 0.00 g) Pressure: 14.7 psi Oxygen %: 21% 1. Executive Summary & Facility Overview The Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II / PSI-117) investigation evaluated the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) aboard the International Space Station. In normal terrestrial gravity (1g), buoyancy draws cool, dense air into the flame base while hot combustion products rise rapidly, creating flickering upward flame spread. In the microgravity environment of the ISS (10^-6 g), buoyant natural convection is eliminated. As a result, molecular diffusion governs oxidizer supply, yielding distinctive hemispherical and soot-free flame structures. 2. Opposed Flow Dynamics & Extinction Limits BASS-II tested polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) solid rods (1.27 cm and 0.635 cm diameter) and cotton-fiberglass blends under controlled forced convective flows ranging from 0 cm/s up to 55 cm/s at 14.7 psi total pressure and 21% oxygen. The experimental data revealed a non-monotonic flame spread curve. At moderate opposed velocities (15 to 30 cm/s), forced airflow continuously replenished oxygen without cooling the pyrolyzing solid, accelerating flame spread. However, below 10 cm/s, flame temperatures dropped as radiative heat loss from CO2 and H2O exceeded reaction enthalpy. At near-quiescent conditions (< 2 cm/s), solid fuels extinguished spontaneously due to stifling by their own combustion products. 3. Fire Safety Calibration for Moon and Mars Missions A critical finding from PSI-117 is that materials passing standard NASA-STD-6001 upward flammability tests on Earth can remain flammable at lower forced flow velocities in microgravity due to longer solid residence times in the preheat zone. Furthermore, spherical blue cool flames (~600 K to 800 K) can persist invisibly after apparent luminous extinction, underscoring the necessity of dual-band infrared sensors in space habitat ventilation ducts.

payload.title: Large-Scale SIBAL Cotton-Fiberglass Flame Spread in ISS-Equivalent Cabin Air
payload.excerpt: Full-scale 0.4 m x 0.9 m SIBAL cotton-fiberglass cloth burned at 20 cm/s airflow exhibited ~1.4x faster flame spread than small-scale glovebox predictions.
payload.text: Saffire-I burned a full-scale 0.4 m by 0.9 m Cotton-Fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric panel inside an uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft at 14.7 psi and 21% O2 with a steady 20 cm/s ventilation flow. Without buoyancy-driven convection in 0g, hot combustion gases remained close to the fabric surface, lengthening the radiative preheat zone and producing a flame spread rate approximately 1.4x higher than small-sample predictions from NASA-STD-6001B 1g upward flame tests.

payload.title: Nasa Psi Cyg Saffire Iv Exploration Atmospheres - Section 1
payload.excerpt: NASA Saffire-IV: Spacecraft Fire Safety in Exploration Atmospheres Elevated Oxygen (30% O2) and Reduced Total Pressure (10.2 psi) Combustion Telemetry for Artemis Moon Base Experiment: Saffire-IV Exploration Atmosphere Environment: Moon Base / Exploration Habitat (10.2 psi, 30...
payload.text: NASA Saffire-IV: Spacecraft Fire Safety in Exploration Atmospheres Elevated Oxygen (30% O2) and Reduced Total Pressure (10.2 psi) Combustion Telemetry for Artemis Moon Base Experiment: Saffire-IV Exploration Atmosphere Environment: Moon Base / Exploration Habitat (10.2 psi, 30% O2, 0.165 g equivalent) Pressure: 10.2 psi Oxygen %: 30% 1. Mission Context & Exploration Atmosphere Rationale Future lunar surface habitats and Artemis pressurized rovers will operate at a reduced cabin pressure of 10.2 psi (70.3 kPa) and an elevated oxygen concentration of 30% (70% N2 diluent). This exploration atmosphere significantly reduces the nitrogen pre-breathe time required for astronauts embarking on Extravehicular Activity (EVA) spacewalks while maintaining an equivalent alveolar oxygen partial pressure (PiO2 approx 21 kPa). However, reducing inert nitrogen diluent fundamentally alters thermal capacitance and microgravity flame propagation. 2. Saffire-IV Large-Scale Combustion Results Conducted inside the pressurized volume of an uncrewed Cygnus resupply vehicle after unberthing from the ISS, Saffire-IV ignited full-scale composite fabrics and 5 cm thick PMMA slabs under forced flow at 10.2 psi and 30% O2. The reduction in convective heat dissipation combined with elevated oxygen concentration produced a 1.42x increase in flame spread velocity compared to sea-level Earth air (14.7 psi / 21% O2). The minimum ignition energy (MIE) decreased from 0.92 mJ to 0.48 mJ, demonstrating that common aerospace polymers ignite under much lower electrical discharge thresholds. 3. Engineering Guidelines for Lunar Habitat Habitation Structural design for lunar base modules must account for the wider flammability boundary of exploration atmospheres. Active fire suppression protocols must account for the reduced effectiveness of Halon-replacement gaseous extinguishants under low convective transport. Ventilation airspeeds must be strictly capped below 15 cm/s during fire alarms to prevent forced-convective acceleration of smoldering insulation.

payload.title: Nasa Std 6001B Spacesuit Eva Pure Oxygen Safety - Section 1
payload.excerpt: NASA-STD-6001B: Flammability Limits in Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) Environments Polymer Wire Insulation, Fasteners, and Arc-Ignition Sensitivity in 4.3 psi Pure Oxygen (100% O2) Experiment: Spacesuit EMU Pure-O2 Screening Environment: Spacesuit EVA (4.3 psi, 100% O2, 0....
payload.text: NASA-STD-6001B: Flammability Limits in Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) Environments Polymer Wire Insulation, Fasteners, and Arc-Ignition Sensitivity in 4.3 psi Pure Oxygen (100% O2) Experiment: Spacesuit EMU Pure-O2 Screening Environment: Spacesuit EVA (4.3 psi, 100% O2, 0.00 g) Pressure: 4.3 psi Oxygen %: 100% 1. Pure Oxygen Environment Dynamics NASA Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) and planetary surface exploration spacesuits operate at 4.3 psi (29.6 kPa) pure 100% oxygen with 0% nitrogen diluent to maximize mobility and prevent decompression sickness. In this environment, the complete absence of inert nitrogen means all chemical heat release is absorbed solely by the reactants and fuel, resulting in adiabatic flame temperatures exceeding 3100 K. 2. Wire Insulation & Polymer Ignition Thresholds Testing under NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 (upward flame propagation) and Test 4 (electrical arc tracking) indicates that standard electrical insulation materials (including PVC, polyurethane, and unmodified Nomex) ignite with a minimum ignition energy of only 0.14 mJ. Flame spread acceleration is approximately 2.38x higher than 14.7 psi atmospheric air. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE / Teflon) and cross-linked ETFE (Tefzel) exhibit extreme resistance, but can support propagating fires if exposed to sustained electrical arcing or titanium friction sparks. 3. Critical Safety Recommendations & Lessons Learned Following historical lessons from the Apollo 1 command module fire and the Apollo 13 cryogenic oxygen tank incident, all spacesuit avionics operating within 4.3 psi 100% O2 must maintain physical hermetic isolation or conformal potting. Materials allowed inside pressurized spacesuit layers must comply with strict limiting oxygen index (LOI) thresholds and zero-g quiescent self-extinguishment verifications.

payload.title: Wire Insulation & Polymer Ignition Sensitivity in 4.3 psi / 100% Oxygen
payload.excerpt: At 4.3 psi and 100% O2, absence of nitrogen diluent drops minimum ignition energy to 0.14 mJ and multiplies polymer flame spread by ~2.38x over 14.7 psi air.
payload.text: Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) spacesuits operate at 4.3 psi pure oxygen (100% O2, 0% N2). Because no inert nitrogen is present to absorb reaction enthalpy, FEP/PTFE wire insulation, hook-and-loop fasteners, and Nomex fabrics face elevated arc-ignition risk (minimum ignition energy ~0.14 mJ) and ~2.38x flame spread acceleration compared to ISS sea-level air. Echoing Apollo 13's Tank 2 PTFE wire-arc lessons, NASA-STD-6001B strictly prohibits unshielded polymer exposure inside 100% O2 enclosures.

payload.experiment: FLEX & ACME (Flame Extinguishment & Cool Flame Investigations)
payload.title: Spherical Diffusion Cool Flames, Droplet Extinction & Electric-Field Flame Control
payload.environmentLabel: Orbital & Moon Base Envelopes (10.2-14.7 psi, 21-30% O2)
payload.excerpt: FLEX and ACME confirmed that zero-buoyancy droplet and gaseous flames stabilize into spherical blue cool-flame zones (~600 K) governed by molecular diffusion and radiative loss.
payload.text: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) and ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) suites aboard the ISS demonstrated that in 0g, elimination of natural convection produces spherically symmetric diffusion flames rather than flickering teardrops. During FLEX droplet tests, heptane and methanol flames extinguished visibly yet continued burning as dim, soot-free spherical cool flames (~600 K) driven by radical chemistry—posing a stealth fire detection challenge for Moon Base and orbital spacecraft habitats.
